kp.k: GCs must govern AI while demonstrating personal adoption
kp.d: Bassli identifies AI as the dominant 2026 GC priority, alongside longstanding concerns about external counsel engagement, billing and spend management, and contracting. She describes an intellectual tension between advising on enterprise-wide AI governance and compliance and showcasing the legal department's own use.
qs: There's always the same priorities we've had for two-plus decades, at least that I've been around this.
GC priorities I think is threading the needle between advisor on governance and compliance of AI- Mm ... and being a user.
And, and showcasing how the legal team is using it.

kp.k: Adoption priorities shift toward demonstrating usage and value
kp.d: Bassli characterizes AI as table stakes for law departments in 2026, with departments ranging from initial adoption to testing and optimization. She contrasts the previous year's exploration with a current focus on actual usage and value. These are practitioner observations, not survey findings or measured adoption rates.
qs: It's now a part of every law department in some way.
They've either initiated the journey and they're at the starting stage, or they're optimizing and testing, or they've got licenses to five different systems and they're tweaking and checking.
I think last year was we're getting in, we're, we're looking into it.
Now the priority's demonstrating usage, demonstrating value.

kp.k: Implementation pressure is outpacing AI strategy
kp.d: Asked whether GCs have defined implementation strategies, Bassli says she cannot affirm this across GCs generally. She observes a significant strategy gap and reactive implementation that could produce poor decisions, noting that some GCs lack legal operations support and resources.
qs: There are a lot of well-intended GCs who don't have the resources, they don't have legal ops
I don't think there are many strategies yet.
In fact, a lot of what we're seeing is a significant gap in strategy and more of a fast move to do
So I'd say we're falling behind on strategy.

kp.k: Executive expectations and unofficial usage squeeze legal leadership
kp.d: Bassli describes top-down pressure from executives who see contract review promoted as an AI application, alongside bottom-up pressure from business colleagues already using AI and bringing its outputs to legal. She says personal phones enable use outside enterprise controls, complicating governance. Her suggestion that GCs and CIOs face the most pressure is explicitly a hunch.
qs: I think the pressure's coming down and seeping in from the bottom.
Because guess what the C-suite sees every first example from every legal AI tool is contract review.
They're using AI to come to legal with their own thoughts already
And they're, by the way, doing it outside of the enterprise tools.
So they are not even using their work laptops because let's say IT tried to lock it down, and they did, and you only have access to whatever they allow you to, it's in their pockets.

kp.k: Develop strategy alongside controlled experimentation, not operational pauses
kp.d: Bassli argues that in-house workloads make stopping work to develop an AI strategy impractical. She recommends demonstrating progress while planning, slowing additional tool acquisition, and experimenting first with an already-authorized enterprise system. She presents legal operations as well suited to managing implementation and strategy in parallel.
qs: Taking a step back is hard, so stop everything and let's think is not a winning approach.
Stepping back is nearly impossible, so how do you in parallel show progress while developing the strategy?
slow down with the new tools, slow down with adding more tools.
Start experimenting and playing with it as you're developing a strategy in parallel.

kp.k: Provide a protected baseline before expanding AI procurement
kp.d: Where no authorized system exists, Bassli recommends giving everyone a common protected enterprise AI environment. For Office 365 organizations, she specifically recommends testing Copilot for a year rather than immediately pursuing add-ons. Her rationale is to create room for learning and strategy development; Kincannon separately suggests this could reduce, but not eliminate, personal-phone use outside the enterprise.
qs: everybody access to some common baseline protected space
if you're already an Office 365 shop, don't go looking for plugins and add-ins and doohickeys.
Just light up Copilot for now, suck it up for a year, and test it.
You can't develop a strategy for something you don't understand.

kp.k: Legal operations must coach GCs to lead by using
kp.d: Bassli argues that adoption mandates alone are insufficient: GCs must demonstrate their own AI experiences to maintain credibility and encourage their teams. Drawing partly on client experiences, she recommends that legal operations leaders have candid conversations with GCs and guide them through experimentation, including low-stakes personal uses, sharing mistakes and showing humility.
qs: Legal ops is the change maker. They're the change driver, in many ways.
The GC then has to demonstrate their own experiences with AI.
In order to be an effective leader in today's age, you cannot be a mandator only.
Demonstrate with some humility, make some mistakes, and share your stories.
I think the legal ops function is to educate the GC that they have a slightly different job to do this time around.

kp.k: AI diffusion limits traditional corporate control over technological change
kp.d: Bassli contrasts AI adoption with the earlier shift to cloud computing. She argues that GCs could previously delay change by retaining on-premises systems, whereas widespread AI use is happening outside the control of the GC and company. This is her explanation for why AI requires a different leadership and change-management approach.
qs: This change isn't like the others.
This is happening, and it isn't in the GC's control. It isn't in the control of the company.
The GC had a big role there and all that, but they could also say no, and they kept stuff on-prem longer than they should have

kp.k: Effective AI use requires iterative interaction rather than one-shot testing
kp.d: Bassli recommends interacting with AI analogously to a junior new hire: explaining, correcting and refining rather than treating it as conventional software with a fixed input-output relationship. Kincannon recommends asking questions, assessing responses and asking better follow-ups. Bassli compares variation in AI responses with variation between lawyers' advice and contract redlines, arguing against dismissing AI after one disappointing result. These are practical analogies and recommendations, not measured performance comparisons.
qs: if you talk to it like you would talk to a new hire At any level in their career, a junior ideally, right? A junior new hire in your department, and treat it that way, not like a tool.
it is a ask a question, assess what was delivered, and then ask another question.
It's a conversation that leads to what you're looking for.
If you ask two attorneys to review a contract, you're gonna get two completely different red line versions.
And yet we're okay with that, and we're so unforgiving with AI.

kp.k: Leadership responses to AI may redirect legal careers
kp.d: Bassli predicts organizational tensions and career movement where leaders mandate AI without authentically engaging or supporting curious staff. Referring to reported career-breaking CLM implementations as an analogy, she expects the broader AI transformation to shape careers, especially those of GCs, through how people handle change rather than through the job-elimination narrative she rejects.
qs: I think we're gonna see a lot of tensions.
We've heard people had career breakers trying to implement CLM.
I think this transformation Is really gonna affect people's career paths
it's gonna do away with your job nonsense.
it will make and redirect careers in the way people handle it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Lucy Bassli describes AI as a baseline resource for corporate legal departments that changes GC responsibilities, adoption strategy, leadership requirements and career trajectories.
pts.d: Bassli claims that AI is now part of every law department in some form, shifting the priority from investigating adoption to demonstrating usage and value. GCs must simultaneously advise on enterprise AI governance and visibly use AI themselves. She sees adoption outpacing strategy, with pressure from executives seeking legal use cases, especially contract review, and employees already using AI outside enterprise controls. She argues that this widespread personal access makes AI adoption less controllable than earlier technological changes such as migration to the cloud. Her recommended response is to experiment with an existing authorized enterprise tool while developing strategy, rather than halt work or accumulate more tools. She argues that GCs must demonstrate hands-on use rather than merely mandate adoption, and that legal operations must coach them and drive departmental change. She presents conversational, iterative interaction with AI as more productive than treating it as a conventional one-input/one-output software tool. She predicts leadership tensions and career changes based on how people handle adoption, explicitly distinguishing that prediction from a claim that AI will eliminate their jobs.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Bassli's professional experience, consulting observations, conference discussions and personal AI experimentation, not quantitative research.
pts.d: Bassli grounds her perspective in more than 13 years in-house at Microsoft and Snowflake and her current legal operations and contracting consultancy. She refers to patterns seen in client organizations, conversations with GCs, and discussions at the conference. Her account of leadership disengagement specifically draws on clients she has worked with. Her discussion of AI interaction draws on her own experimentation, including repeated instructions and asking the system why it consulted a file. Analogies to teenagers using technology beyond parental control and to training a junior hire explain her reasoning but are not empirical tests. The transcript offers no adoption survey, measured productivity improvement, benchmark or documented career outcome supporting the generalizations. She explicitly labels the claim that GCs and CIOs face the greatest pressure as her hunch. The sponsor's product claims are separate from her analysis.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern the 2026 adoption environment; future career effects are undated, and implementation advice depends on existing tools and organizational support.
pts.d: Speaking at the 2026 conference, Bassli contrasts the current emphasis on usage and value with the previous year's exploration. She qualifies her universal adoption claim by describing departments at very different stages, from starting out to testing several systems. Although asked about 2026–2027 and the next year or two, she does not offer a dated forecast of new priorities beyond AI, spend management and contracting. Strategy development must proceed alongside ongoing work because in-house operations cannot simply stop. If an enterprise tool is already authorized, she recommends using it first; for an Office 365 organization, she suggests trying Copilot for a year before adding products. Where no tool is available, she recommends supplying a common protected enterprise option, while acknowledging that employees may already be using personal devices. Her advice that legal operations should challenge and coach the GC assumes a close working relationship and the existence of that function. Predictions of tensions and redirected careers have no specified deadline or quantified scale.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate GCs, legal operations professionals, legal department staff and business employees, rather than law-firm staffing markets or the public.
pts.d: GCs acquire a dual governance-and-user responsibility and face expectations from executives and AI-using employees. CIOs also face pressure to govern and enable use. Legal operations professionals become implementation leaders and coaches who must secure authentic GC participation. Departments without legal operations resources face a greater burden on the GC to manage adoption personally. Legal team members' engagement and career paths may be affected by leaders' openness to experimentation. Business employees are both sources of adoption pressure and intended users of approved enterprise environments. Contracting is especially visible because contract review is prominent in vendor demonstrations seen by executives. Bassli does not develop a concrete prediction about law-firm pricing, staffing displacement, ALSP competition or access to justice; the proposed return to law-firm engagement does not become a substantive discussion.
